cards.title: Evolution of Modern Java
cards.content:
Since Java 9, Oracle transitioned to a strict 6-month release cadence. This means new features are delivered much faster through rapid feature releases, alongside Long-Term Support (LTS) releases every 2 years (starting with Java 17).

Key highlights of modern Java versions include:

  • Java 8: Lambdas, Streams, and Optional
  • Java 11: HTTP Client, String APIs, and run single-file source code
  • Java 17: Sealed Classes, Pattern Matching (Preview), and Records
  • Java 21: Virtual Threads, Pattern Matching for switch, and Sequenced Collections

cards.title: Lambda Expressions & Functional Interfaces
cards.content:
Introduced in Java 8, Lambda Expressions allow you to treat functionality as a method argument, or code as data. A lambda expression can only implement a Functional Interface (an interface with exactly one abstract method).

// Traditional anonymous class
Runnable r1 = new Runnable() {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Hello World");
    }
};

// Modern Lambda expression
Runnable r2 = () -> System.out.println("Hello World");

An interface that has been declared abstract but contains no methods.
An interface with no abstract methods and one private method.

cards.title: The Streams API
cards.content:
The Streams API provides a declarative way to process collections of objects. A stream pipeline consists of a source, zero or more intermediate operations, and a terminal operation.

Intermediate Operations are lazy and return a new stream (e.g., filter(), map(), sorted()). Terminal Operations trigger processing and produce a result or side-effect (e.g., collect(), forEach(), reduce()).

List<String> names = List.of("Anna", "Bob", "Alex", "Charlie");

List<String> filtered = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("A"))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// Output: ["ANNA", "ALEX"]

items.text: Obtain a stream from a data source (e.g., list.stream())
Transform elements using intermediate mappings (e.g., map(mapper))
Apply a terminal operation (e.g., collect()) to trigger lazy evaluation and compile final results

cards.title: Local Variable Type Inference (var)
cards.content:
Introduced in Java 10, the var keyword allows local variable type inference. The compiler infers the exact type based on the initialization value.

// Instead of:
Map<String, List<Integer>> map = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

// You can write:
var map = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

Crucial Rules:

  • Only works inside local blocks (methods, loops, try-with-resources).
  • Cannot be used for member fields, method parameters, or return types.
  • Must have an explicit initializer statement.

cards.title: Records & Sealed Classes
cards.content:
Modern Java introduces powerful object-oriented constructs to represent clean data carriers and manage subclass hierarchies:

Records (Java 16): Immutable data classes that generate boilerplate code (getters, constructors, toString, equals, and hashCode) automatically.

public record User(String username, String email) {}

Sealed Classes (Java 17): Restricts which classes or interfaces may extend or implement them using the sealed and permits modifiers.

public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Square {}
public final class Circle extends Shape {}
public final class Square extends Shape {}

cards.title: Pattern Matching for switch
cards.content:
With modern pattern matching, you can check object types and bind matching values to variables directly inside switch expressions, making boilerplate-heavy instanceof checks obsolete.

static String formatterPatternSwitch(Object obj) {
    return switch (obj) {
        case Integer i -> String.format("int %d", i);
        case Long l    -> String.format("long %d", l);
        case Double d  -> String.format("double %f", d);
        case String s  -> String.format("String %s", s);
        default        -> obj.toString();
    };
}

options.text: Permitted subclasses must be defined within the same file without exception.
Every permitted subclass of a sealed class must explicitly use one of: final, sealed, or non-sealed modifiers.
Any subclass extending a sealed class is automatically marked final by the compiler.
Permitted subclasses must implement all default interfaces implemented by the parent.
